UC Davis Aggies are the athletic teams of the University of California, Davis, featuring a white mustang as their emblem, and their mascot image can be traced back to the 1920s. The university announced on December 10, 2024, that it had accepted an invitation to join the Mountain West Conference beginning July 1, 2026, while football will remain in the Big Sky Conference. The men's basketball team won the 1998 NCAA Division II National Championship, along with the 2015 and 2018 Big West Conference regular-season championships and the 2017 conference tournament championship.
2
Team history
The conference affiliations of the UC Davis Aggies men's basketball team were, in order, the Far West Conference (1925–1982), the Northern California Athletic Conference (1982–1998), the California Collegiate Athletic Association (1998–2004), Division I Independent (2004–2007), and the
Big West Conference
(2007–present); the 2025–26 season is the team's 19th season competing in the Big West.
5
On December 10, 2024, UC Davis accepted a formal invitation from the Mountain West Conference and will join the conference on July 1, 2026. Beginning with the 2026–27 season, UC Davis will compete in all Mountain West-sponsored sports, while football will remain in the Big Sky Conference in the FCS; men's and women's water polo and beach volleyball will seek to remain in the Big West as affiliate members and explore other options if necessary; membership agreements for equestrian, field hockey, and lacrosse will remain unchanged.
2
Roster

The returning core of the UC Davis Aggies men's basketball team includes Brayden Fagbemi, Connor Sevilla, Isaiah Chappell, Omer Suljanovic, Jalen Stokes, Chase Rawlins, and Ylan Esso-Essis. The six returning players who saw game action combined for 1,244 points, nearly half of the team's total scoring. The seven returning players helped the team post a 19-14 record and a 12-4 home record at University Credit Union Center. Head coach Jim Les said that this returning group is the foundation of the team, bringing leadership, experience, and resilience.
1
In his junior season, Connor Sevilla averaged 13.3 points and 31.2 minutes per game and earned All-Big West honorable mention. He led the Big West with a 90.3% free-throw percentage, ranked 12th nationally, made a team-high 67 three-pointers with a 39.9% three-point percentage, and twice went 11-for-11 from the free-throw line in a single game. Against North Dakota State, Sevilla scored a career-high 26 points, shooting 8-for-10 from the field and making 6 three-pointers; in the final moments of the first round of the Big West Tournament, he made 8 consecutive free throws to help the team defeat UC Santa Barbara 79-73; he also earned CSC Academic All-District for the second consecutive year and was named to the NABC Honors Court.
1

Brayden Fagbemi led the Big West with 2.0 steals per game, ranking 36th nationally; his 133 assists and 4.3 assists per game both ranked second in the conference, and despite starting only 3 games, he still led the team in assists and steals while also averaging 3.5 rebounds per game. In the final regular-season road game at UC Irvine, Fagbemi scored a season-high 16 points and recorded 5 steals, and was named to the CSC Academic All-District and NABC Honors Court. Previously at Central Arkansas, he averaged 11.4 points, 4.7 assists, 4.1 rebounds, and 1.5 steals per game; earlier at Johns Hopkins, he earned D3hoops.com Region V and Centennial Conference Rookie of the Year honors.
1
Isaiah Chappell, at 2.06 meters tall, was one of only two Aggies to play in all 33 games; as a sophomore, he started 18 games and averaged 8.5 points and 4.6 rebounds, led the team with 135 defensive rebounds, and ranked second on the team with 58 three-pointers. He scored a season-high 20 points against Seattle U, made 4 three-pointers in a single game five times, and in a road game against Nevada scored 9 points, grabbed a team-high 6 rebounds, and hit a three-pointer during a closing 9-0 run.
1

Omer Suljanovic appeared in 32 games and started 9, averaging 5.6 points and 3.0 rebounds while shooting 37.0% from three-point range in Big West games. He scored a season-high 13 points on 5-of-7 shooting against Sacramento State, grabbed a season-high 13 rebounds, and scored 10 points in the season finale against Cal State Fullerton at the Big West Tournament. Jalen Stokes appeared in 27 games and started 7, averaging 4.7 points and 2.5 rebounds while shooting 44.8% from the field; the 1.96-meter guard shot 87.8% from the free-throw line, second among Aggie regulars behind Sevilla, and shot 88.9% from the free-throw line in conference games. He scored a season-high 17 points against Pacific Union and scored 16 points on 10-of-10 free-throw shooting against UC Riverside.
1
Niko Rocak is entering his third season at UC Davis, averaging 6.8 rebounds per game, and has set program records with 58 blocks in a single season and 6 blocks in a single game. He has represented the Switzerland U20 national team and has made his debut for the senior national team; after earning a degree in chemistry, he is pursuing an MBA.
5
In terms of international background and family legacy, Nils Cooper represents the Sweden U18 national team and is the son of Hall of Famer
Michael Cooper
. Isaiah Chappell represents the New Zealand U18 national team and is the son of Mike Chappell, who won an NCAA championship with Michigan State and played in the Australian NBL. Ylan Esso-Essis is from France and developed in the Metropolitans 92 program; Jonathan Noudjihidi was born in N'Djamena, Chad. Omer Suljanovic is from Vienna, Austria, and made his senior national team debut at age 17; Abdullah Amzil is from Finland and was named Finnish U19 Player of the Year.
7
Management team

Jim Les serves as head coach of the UC Davis Aggies men's basketball team. As of February 2026, he has recorded 128 Big West wins, ranks seventh in conference history, and is one of three active Big West coaches with 100 or more conference wins. He has 226 total wins at UC Davis and surpassed Jerry Pimm on January 31, 2026.
17
Head coach Jim Les, associate head coach Kevin Nosek, and assistant coaches Kyle Vogt and Jonathan Metzger-Jones have worked together since the 2016-17 season, forming the longest-tenured coaching staff in NCAA Division I men's basketball. Assistant coach Kyle Vogt was named to the Silver Waves Media Top 100 Mid-Major Assistant Coaches and GMs and is in his 14th season with the program. Under his guidance, the UC Davis defense ranked among the national top 50 in forced turnovers in six of the past eight seasons.
6
For the 2025-26 season, the coaching staff added Fortune Solomon, Mike Kosich, and Reece Lakritz. Fortune Solomon serves as an assistant coach; he previously worked for the Long Island Nets, the NBA G League affiliate of the Brooklyn Nets, and served as an assistant coach for the South Sudan national team, helping the team qualify for the Olympics for the first time. Mike Kosich serves as an assistant coach and chief of staff; he previously worked at San Diego State and South Alabama and has experience in roster construction, scouting, and day-to-day operations. Reece Lakritz is a UC Davis student and former team manager, serving as video coordinator and assistant director of basketball operations, and has been part of the Aggie program since 2023.
9
Team home venue
University Credit Union Center is the home venue for UC Davis men's basketball, women's basketball, women's volleyball, and women's gymnastics. In July 2021, UC Davis and University Credit Union entered into a ten-year partnership, and the venue was renamed from The Pavilion to University Credit Union Center.
10

On July 20, 2021, signage installation was completed at University Credit Union Center. Full-name signage was installed at the northeast corner of the main entrance, and abbreviated “U Center” signage was installed at the southeast and southwest corners. “Pavilion District” in wayfinding signage was changed to “U Center District,” while the name Pavilion Parking Structure remained unchanged. The venue is equipped with a Daktronics video board more than 13 feet high and 46 feet wide, capable of showing replays and real-time statistics.
11
University Credit Union Center opened for the 1977–78 season, has a basketball capacity of 6,003, and is one of the largest campus basketball arenas in Northern California. In the first official basketball game on November 26, 1977, 2,600 spectators saw the University of the Pacific defeat the Aggies 78–69. On December 9, 1995, the basketball court inside the venue was named Hamilton Court in honor of former men's basketball head coach Bob Hamilton.
10
After the venue was reconfigured in 2009, the five highest-attendance games were all nationally televised UC Davis home games. The men's basketball program's all-time attendance record is 7,926, set in a game against Chico State, and cannot be reached under the current configuration; the women's basketball attendance record is 4,712.
10
The Activities and Recreation Center is connected to the University Credit Union Center. Aggie Stadium began hosting football and women's lacrosse games in 2007, with an initial seating capacity of approximately 10,000 and plans to expand to 30,000. La Rue Field is a softball field with a seating capacity of approximately 300; it underwent a major renovation before the 2018 season and was named the Sports Turf Managers Association's Softball Field of the Year in January 1999. The Schaal Aquatics Center hosted its first event in January 2004 and features an Olympic-size pool and approximately 500 permanent seats. The Aggie Field Hockey Facility held its first event on August 23, 2014.
10
Statistics

In the 2025–26 season, the UC Davis men's basketball team established its identity around efficiency and defensive pressure. That season, UC Davis went 8–0 when holding opponents below 40% shooting, 14–1 when its shooting percentage was higher than its opponent's, 15–6 when allowing 79 points or fewer, 8–1 when scoring 80 points or more, and 11–6 when leading at halftime.
3
UC Davis forced 14.94 turnovers per game, ranking 14th nationally, and had a turnover margin of +2.1, ranking 31st nationally and leading the Big West. UC Davis averaged 8.0 steals per game, second in the conference, and ranked ninth nationally in non-steal turnover rate. UC Davis averaged 15.7 assists per game, ranking 80th nationally, and ranked 28th nationally in assist rate.
3
In the 2025–26 season, UC Davis had a 12–3 home record at University Credit Union Center, went 8–3 in white uniforms, and went 3–1 in Tahoe Blue uniforms. On March 8, 2025, UC Davis men's basketball defeated UC San Diego 69–58 at LionTree Arena, with quarter scores of 14–18, 8–13, 18–16, and 29–11. In that game, UC Davis shot 50% (24–48) from the field, 37% (10–27) from three-point range, and 79% (11–14) from the free-throw line, grabbed 30 rebounds, committed 14 turnovers, led by as many as 11 points, and had an attendance of 472.
15

As of October 18, 2026, the UC Davis Aggies football team had a 5–3 record in the 2026 season, a 3–2 record in Big Sky play, and ranked fourth in the conference. The team averaged 275.0 passing yards per game (40th nationally), 166.6 rushing yards per game (44th), 32.0 points per game (tied for 29th), and 31.0 points allowed per game (85th). Individual statistical leaders included Treynor Cleeland with 1,981 passing yards and 16 touchdowns; Jordan Fisher with 847 rushing yards, 127 carries, and 10 touchdowns; and Samuel Gbatu Jr. with 830 receiving yards, 58 receptions, and 5 touchdowns.
18
Team Honors
The UC Davis Aggies men's basketball team won the 1998 NCAA Division II National Championship and has made 12 appearances in the NCAA regional tournament, winning the 2015 and 2018 Big West regular-season championships, the 2017 Big West Tournament championship, and earning berths in the 2017 NCAA Tournament and the 2015 and 2018 NIT. The UC Davis Aggies have had seven seasons with a winning percentage above .500 and multiple 20-win seasons; in 2014–15, they set a Division I program record with 25 wins, and in 2017, the team defeated NC Central in the NCAA Tournament First Four to record the first NCAA Division I tournament win in program history.
3
The team has defeated Utah State, California, Oregon State, Washington State, and Grand Canyon, including a 75–68 road win over Grand Canyon that ended the opponent's then 18-game home winning streak. At the time, Grand Canyon's home winning streak was one of the longest in the nation.
3

In the 2017 Big West Tournament championship game, the UC Davis Aggies defeated UC Irvine 50–47 to advance to the NCAA Division I Men's Basketball Tournament for the first time in program history; Brynton Lemar was named to the All-Tournament Team, and Chima Moneke was named the tournament's Most Valuable Player. In the NCAA Tournament, Chima Moneke scored a team-high 20 points, Brynton Lemar contributed 17 points and 3 steals, Siler Schneider scored 10 points, and the team ultimately lost to Kansas, ending the season.
20
Alumni include 2023 EuroCup MVP T.J. Shorts II; EuroCup MVP and former Sacramento Kings player Chima Moneke; Elijah Pepper, who plays for the Perth Wildcats; Brynton Lemar, who plays in Europe; Ezra Manjon, who plays in Italy; and A.J. John, who plays in Japan, Belgium, Israel, and Mexico. Other alumni include Corey Hawkins, who serves as an assistant coach for the Orlando Magic; Joe Harden, founder of Salty Goats Winery; Mark Payne, vice president at Morgan Stanley; Ryan Howley, vice president at Bessemer Trust; and Ryan Sypkens and Justin Dueck, entrepreneurs.
3
In fall 2024, all eight UC Davis fall varsity teams qualified for postseason play. The men's soccer team won the Big West championship and advanced to the NCAA Tournament; the football team reached the FCS playoffs and earned the No. 5 national seed; the women's soccer and women's cross country teams finished second in the Big West; the men's water polo, men's cross country, and women's indoor volleyball teams finished third in the Big West; and the field hockey team finished sixth in America East.
2
Team Culture

UC Davis's white mustang mascot can be traced back to the 1920s. The new athletics logo centers on the white mustang and symbolizes dignity, class, strength, pride, quality, honesty, tradition, teamwork, and a drive to forge ahead. In the primary logo, the horse's silhouette is encircled by a blue horseshoe-shaped letter C against a gold background, with "UC Davis Aggies" printed in bold blue below; secondary marks include a horse head viewed from another angle, a running horse with "Go Ags!", and a cartoon version for children. The mustang became a UC Davis symbol in connection with the U.S. Army bringing the Thoroughbred Gunrock to campus in 1921, and Aggie students later chose the mustang to commemorate Gunrock's renown.
4
UC Davis team culture emphasizes defense, competition, and a tough-game mentality. During the 2017 Big West Tournament championship run, head coach Jim Les said the team brought a "hard-hat mentality" to every game, defense won those games, and the players displayed competitive greatness. The players have good habits, work hard, work together, hold each other accountable, and respect all opponents in preparation.
3
UC Davis men's basketball remains the academic standard-bearer in the Big West, with a 98% graduation rate and a team GPA above 3.0.
8
After the 2017 NCAA Tournament, the Sacramento area expressed support through television, radio, and newspaper interviews, and the Sacramento Kings and Sacramento River Cats honored the men's and women's basketball programs before and during home games; in the same season, the women's basketball team also achieved a historic WNIT Sweet 16 result.
3
Related events
On September 19, 2026, the UC Davis Aggies football team defeated the Stetson Hatters 45–7; Zach Jones scored two punt-return touchdowns, and Treynor Cleeland threw two touchdown passes; UC Davis totaled 498 yards, with an attendance of 15,270.
22

On December 7, 2024, the UC Davis Aggies football team defeated Illinois State 42–10 in the second round of the FCS playoffs; Miles Hastings completed 25 of 33 passes for 3 touchdowns, and Lan Larison scored on 1-yard, 27-yard, and 2-yard rushing touchdowns; UC Davis led in total yards 560 to 412, with an attendance of 6,317.

## Former varsity sports
[edit]
On April 20, 2010, the school announced that four sports, women's rowing, men's swimming and diving, men's indoor track and field, and wrestling, would be eliminated due to a financial crisis and cuts in state funding.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UC_Davis_Aggies#cite_note-30)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UC_Davis_Aggies#cite_note-sacbee1-2)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UC_Davis_Aggies#cite_note-31)
Prior to 2010, the last time UC Davis had discontinued a sport was men's gymnastics in 1987.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UC_Davis_Aggies#cite_note-32)
Colby "Babe" Slater, won gold medals with the U.S. rugby national team at the 1920 and 1924 Olympics, and was captain of the 1924 team.
The UC Davis Aggies won the men's 2015 DI-AA college rugby championship by defeating Central Florida in the final 18–15 at Kennesaw State University's Fifth Third Bank Stadium.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UC_Davis_Aggies#cite_note-33) The men repeated as the 2016 D1-AA as national champions by defeating the Notre Dame College of South Euclid, Ohio, in the final by a score of 17–13.
The UC Davis Aggies won the women's 2016 D1 college rugby national championship by defeating the University of Virginia, 30–25, at Saint Mary's College in Moraga, California.

UC Davis Aggies are the athletic teams of the University of California, Davis, featuring a white mustang as their emblem, and their mascot image can be traced back to the 1920s. The university announced on December 10, 2024, that it had accepted an invitation to join the Mountain West Conference beginning July 1, 2026, while football will remain in the Big Sky Conference. The men's basketball team won the 1998 NCAA Division II National Championship, along with the 2015 and 2018 Big West Conference regular-season championships and the 2017 conference tournament championship.
2
Team history
The conference affiliations of the UC Davis Aggies men's basketball team were, in order, the Far West Conference (1925–1982), the Northern California Athletic Conference (1982–1998), the California Collegiate Athletic Association (1998–2004), Division I Independent (2004–2007), and the
Big West Conference
(2007–present); the 2025–26 season is the team's 19th season competing in the Big West.
5
On December 10, 2024, UC Davis accepted a formal invitation from the Mountain West Conference and will join the conference on July 1, 2026. Beginning with the 2026–27 season, UC Davis will compete in all Mountain West-sponsored sports, while football will remain in the Big Sky Conference in the FCS; men's and women's water polo and beach volleyball will seek to remain in the Big West as affiliate members and explore other options if necessary; membership agreements for equestrian, field hockey, and lacrosse will remain unchanged.
2
Roster

The returning core of the UC Davis Aggies men's basketball team includes Brayden Fagbemi, Connor Sevilla, Isaiah Chappell, Omer Suljanovic, Jalen Stokes, Chase Rawlins, and Ylan Esso-Essis. The six returning players who saw game action combined for 1,244 points, nearly half of the team's total scoring. The seven returning players helped the team post a 19-14 record and a 12-4 home record at University Credit Union Center. Head coach Jim Les said that this returning group is the foundation of the team, bringing leadership, experience, and resilience.
1
In his junior season, Connor Sevilla averaged 13.3 points and 31.2 minutes per game and earned All-Big West honorable mention. He led the Big West with a 90.3% free-throw percentage, ranked 12th nationally, made a team-high 67 three-pointers with a 39.9% three-point percentage, and twice went 11-for-11 from the free-throw line in a single game. Against North Dakota State, Sevilla scored a career-high 26 points, shooting 8-for-10 from the field and making 6 three-pointers; in the final moments of the first round of the Big West Tournament, he made 8 consecutive free throws to help the team defeat UC Santa Barbara 79-73; he also earned CSC Academic All-District for the second consecutive year and was named to the NABC Honors Court.
1

Brayden Fagbemi led the Big West with 2.0 steals per game, ranking 36th nationally; his 133 assists and 4.3 assists per game both ranked second in the conference, and despite starting only 3 games, he still led the team in assists and steals while also averaging 3.5 rebounds per game. In the final regular-season road game at UC Irvine, Fagbemi scored a season-high 16 points and recorded 5 steals, and was named to the CSC Academic All-District and NABC Honors Court. Previously at Central Arkansas, he averaged 11.4 points, 4.7 assists, 4.1 rebounds, and 1.5 steals per game; earlier at Johns Hopkins, he earned D3hoops.com Region V and Centennial Conference Rookie of the Year honors.
1
Isaiah Chappell, at 2.06 meters tall, was one of only two Aggies to play in all 33 games; as a sophomore, he started 18 games and averaged 8.5 points and 4.6 rebounds, led the team with 135 defensive rebounds, and ranked second on the team with 58 three-pointers. He scored a season-high 20 points against Seattle U, made 4 three-pointers in a single game five times, and in a road game against Nevada scored 9 points, grabbed a team-high 6 rebounds, and hit a three-pointer during a closing 9-0 run.
1

Omer Suljanovic appeared in 32 games and started 9, averaging 5.6 points and 3.0 rebounds while shooting 37.0% from three-point range in Big West games. He scored a season-high 13 points on 5-of-7 shooting against Sacramento State, grabbed a season-high 13 rebounds, and scored 10 points in the season finale against Cal State Fullerton at the Big West Tournament. Jalen Stokes appeared in 27 games and started 7, averaging 4.7 points and 2.5 rebounds while shooting 44.8% from the field; the 1.96-meter guard shot 87.8% from the free-throw line, second among Aggie regulars behind Sevilla, and shot 88.9% from the free-throw line in conference games. He scored a season-high 17 points against Pacific Union and scored 16 points on 10-of-10 free-throw shooting against UC Riverside.
1
Niko Rocak is entering his third season at UC Davis, averaging 6.8 rebounds per game, and has set program records with 58 blocks in a single season and 6 blocks in a single game. He has represented the Switzerland U20 national team and has made his debut for the senior national team; after earning a degree in chemistry, he is pursuing an MBA.

In terms of international background and family legacy, Nils Cooper represents the Sweden U18 national team and is the son of Hall of Famer
Michael Cooper
. Isaiah Chappell represents the New Zealand U18 national team and is the son of Mike Chappell, who won an NCAA championship with Michigan State and played in the Australian NBL. Ylan Esso-Essis is from France and developed in the Metropolitans 92 program; Jonathan Noudjihidi was born in N'Djamena, Chad. Omer Suljanovic is from Vienna, Austria, and made his senior national team debut at age 17; Abdullah Amzil is from Finland and was named Finnish U19 Player of the Year.

Management team

Jim Les serves as head coach of the UC Davis Aggies men's basketball team. As of February 2026, he has recorded 128 Big West wins, ranks seventh in conference history, and is one of three active Big West coaches with 100 or more conference wins. He has 226 total wins at UC Davis and surpassed Jerry Pimm on January 31, 2026.
17
Head coach Jim Les, associate head coach Kevin Nosek, and assistant coaches Kyle Vogt and Jonathan Metzger-Jones have worked together since the 2016-17 season, forming the longest-tenured coaching staff in NCAA Division I men's basketball. Assistant coach Kyle Vogt was named to the Silver Waves Media Top 100 Mid-Major Assistant Coaches and GMs and is in his 14th season with the program. Under his guidance, the UC Davis defense ranked among the national top 50 in forced turnovers in six of the past eight seasons.
6
For the 2025-26 season, the coaching staff added Fortune Solomon, Mike Kosich, and Reece Lakritz. Fortune Solomon serves as an assistant coach; he previously worked for the Long Island Nets, the NBA G League affiliate of the Brooklyn Nets, and served as an assistant coach for the South Sudan national team, helping the team qualify for the Olympics for the first time. Mike Kosich serves as an assistant coach and chief of staff; he previously worked at San Diego State and South Alabama and has experience in roster construction, scouting, and day-to-day operations. Reece Lakritz is a UC Davis student and former team manager, serving as video coordinator and assistant director of basketball operations, and has been part of the Aggie program since 2023.
9
Team home venue
University Credit Union Center is the home venue for UC Davis men's basketball, women's basketball, women's volleyball, and women's gymnastics. In July 2021, UC Davis and University Credit Union entered into a ten-year partnership, and the venue was renamed from The Pavilion to University Credit Union Center.
10

On July 20, 2021, signage installation was completed at University Credit Union Center. Full-name signage was installed at the northeast corner of the main entrance, and abbreviated “U Center” signage was installed at the southeast and southwest corners. “Pavilion District” in wayfinding signage was changed to “U Center District,” while the name Pavilion Parking Structure remained unchanged. The venue is equipped with a Daktronics video board more than 13 feet high and 46 feet wide, capable of showing replays and real-time statistics.
11
University Credit Union Center opened for the 1977–78 season, has a basketball capacity of 6,003, and is one of the largest campus basketball arenas in Northern California. In the first official basketball game on November 26, 1977, 2,600 spectators saw the University of the Pacific defeat the Aggies 78–69. On December 9, 1995, the basketball court inside the venue was named Hamilton Court in honor of former men's basketball head coach Bob Hamilton.
10
After the venue was reconfigured in 2009, the five highest-attendance games were all nationally televised UC Davis home games. The men's basketball program's all-time attendance record is 7,926, set in a game against Chico State, and cannot be reached under the current configuration; the women's basketball attendance record is 4,712.
10
The Activities and Recreation Center is connected to the University Credit Union Center. Aggie Stadium began hosting football and women's lacrosse games in 2007, with an initial seating capacity of approximately 10,000 and plans to expand to 30,000. La Rue Field is a softball field with a seating capacity of approximately 300; it underwent a major renovation before the 2018 season and was named the Sports Turf Managers Association's Softball Field of the Year in January 1999. The Schaal Aquatics Center hosted its first event in January 2004 and features an Olympic-size pool and approximately 500 permanent seats. The Aggie Field Hockey Facility held its first event on August 23, 2014.
10
Statistics

In the 2025–26 season, the UC Davis men's basketball team established its identity around efficiency and defensive pressure. That season, UC Davis went 8–0 when holding opponents below 40% shooting, 14–1 when its shooting percentage was higher than its opponent's, 15–6 when allowing 79 points or fewer, 8–1 when scoring 80 points or more, and 11–6 when leading at halftime.
3
UC Davis forced 14.94 turnovers per game, ranking 14th nationally, and had a turnover margin of +2.1, ranking 31st nationally and leading the Big West. UC Davis averaged 8.0 steals per game, second in the conference, and ranked ninth nationally in non-steal turnover rate. UC Davis averaged 15.7 assists per game, ranking 80th nationally, and ranked 28th nationally in assist rate.
3
In the 2025–26 season, UC Davis had a 12–3 home record at University Credit Union Center, went 8–3 in white uniforms, and went 3–1 in Tahoe Blue uniforms. On March 8, 2025, UC Davis men's basketball defeated UC San Diego 69–58 at LionTree Arena, with quarter scores of 14–18, 8–13, 18–16, and 29–11. In that game, UC Davis shot 50% (24–48) from the field, 37% (10–27) from three-point range, and 79% (11–14) from the free-throw line, grabbed 30 rebounds, committed 14 turnovers, led by as many as 11 points, and had an attendance of 472.
15

As of October 18, 2026, the UC Davis Aggies football team had a 5–3 record in the 2026 season, a 3–2 record in Big Sky play, and ranked fourth in the conference. The team averaged 275.0 passing yards per game (40th nationally), 166.6 rushing yards per game (44th), 32.0 points per game (tied for 29th), and 31.0 points allowed per game (85th). Individual statistical leaders included Treynor Cleeland with 1,981 passing yards and 16 touchdowns; Jordan Fisher with 847 rushing yards, 127 carries, and 10 touchdowns; and Samuel Gbatu Jr. with 830 receiving yards, 58 receptions, and 5 touchdowns.
18
Team Honors
The UC Davis Aggies men's basketball team won the 1998 NCAA Division II National Championship and has made 12 appearances in the NCAA regional tournament, winning the 2015 and 2018 Big West regular-season championships, the 2017 Big West Tournament championship, and earning berths in the 2017 NCAA Tournament and the 2015 and 2018 NIT. The UC Davis Aggies have had seven seasons with a winning percentage above .500 and multiple 20-win seasons; in 2014–15, they set a Division I program record with 25 wins, and in 2017, the team defeated NC Central in the NCAA Tournament First Four to record the first NCAA Division I tournament win in program history.
3
The team has defeated Utah State, California, Oregon State, Washington State, and Grand Canyon, including a 75–68 road win over Grand Canyon that ended the opponent's then 18-game home winning streak. At the time, Grand Canyon's home winning streak was one of the longest in the nation.
3

In the 2017 Big West Tournament championship game, the UC Davis Aggies defeated UC Irvine 50–47 to advance to the NCAA Division I Men's Basketball Tournament for the first time in program history; Brynton Lemar was named to the All-Tournament Team, and Chima Moneke was named the tournament's Most Valuable Player. In the NCAA Tournament, Chima Moneke scored a team-high 20 points, Brynton Lemar contributed 17 points and 3 steals, Siler Schneider scored 10 points, and the team ultimately lost to Kansas, ending the season.
20
Alumni include 2023 EuroCup MVP T.J. Shorts II; EuroCup MVP and former Sacramento Kings player Chima Moneke; Elijah Pepper, who plays for the Perth Wildcats; Brynton Lemar, who plays in Europe; Ezra Manjon, who plays in Italy; and A.J. John, who plays in Japan, Belgium, Israel, and Mexico. Other alumni include Corey Hawkins, who serves as an assistant coach for the Orlando Magic; Joe Harden, founder of Salty Goats Winery; Mark Payne, vice president at Morgan Stanley; Ryan Howley, vice president at Bessemer Trust; and Ryan Sypkens and Justin Dueck, entrepreneurs.
3
In fall 2024, all eight UC Davis fall varsity teams qualified for postseason play. The men's soccer team won the Big West championship and advanced to the NCAA Tournament; the football team reached the FCS playoffs and earned the No. 5 national seed; the women's soccer and women's cross country teams finished second in the Big West; the men's water polo, men's cross country, and women's indoor volleyball teams finished third in the Big West; and the field hockey team finished sixth in America East.
2
Team Culture

UC Davis's white mustang mascot can be traced back to the 1920s. The new athletics logo centers on the white mustang and symbolizes dignity, class, strength, pride, quality, honesty, tradition, teamwork, and a drive to forge ahead. In the primary logo, the horse's silhouette is encircled by a blue horseshoe-shaped letter C against a gold background, with "UC Davis Aggies" printed in bold blue below; secondary marks include a horse head viewed from another angle, a running horse with "Go Ags!", and a cartoon version for children. The mustang became a UC Davis symbol in connection with the U.S. Army bringing the Thoroughbred Gunrock to campus in 1921, and Aggie students later chose the mustang to commemorate Gunrock's renown.
4
UC Davis team culture emphasizes defense, competition, and a tough-game mentality. During the 2017 Big West Tournament championship run, head coach Jim Les said the team brought a "hard-hat mentality" to every game, defense won those games, and the players displayed competitive greatness. The players have good habits, work hard, work together, hold each other accountable, and respect all opponents in preparation.
3
UC Davis men's basketball remains the academic standard-bearer in the Big West, with a 98% graduation rate and a team GPA above 3.0.
8
After the 2017 NCAA Tournament, the Sacramento area expressed support through television, radio, and newspaper interviews, and the Sacramento Kings and Sacramento River Cats honored the men's and women's basketball programs before and during home games; in the same season, the women's basketball team also achieved a historic WNIT Sweet 16 result.
3
Related events
On September 19, 2026, the UC Davis Aggies football team defeated the Stetson Hatters 45–7; Zach Jones scored two punt-return touchdowns, and Treynor Cleeland threw two touchdown passes; UC Davis totaled 498 yards, with an attendance of 15,270.
22

**Fort Hill High School** is a four-year public high school in Cumberland, Maryland, United States, serving 780 students in grades 9 through 12. Fort Hill is part of Allegany County Public Schools**.**
Fort Hill High School was one of three local New Deal projects. Fort Hill High school was a Public Works Administration project. Nearby Constitution Park and Greeway Avenue Stadium were Works Progress Administration projects
New Deal funding relating to Fort Hill was initiated in November 1934 and September 1935, when the PWA committed federal funds not to exceed $230,000. The project was labeled PWA Docket #7323.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_High_School#cite_note-2)

When Fort Hill opened, it had 1763 students and 88 teachers. Heisey was the first principal.

### State championships
[edit]
**Boys Cross Country:**
*   Class 2A 1995, 1997[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_High_School#cite_note-auto1-3)
**Football:**
*   Class 3A 1975 (undefeated)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_High_School#cite_note-auto1-3)  
*   Class 2A 1997 (undefeated)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_High_School#cite_note-auto1-3)  
*   Class 1A 2013 (undefeated), 2014 (undefeated), 2015, 2016 (undefeated), 2018 (undefeated), 2021 (undefeated), 2022, 2023 (undefeated), 2024 [[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_High_School#cite_note-auto1-3)
**Volleyball:**
*   Class 1A 2013[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_High_School#cite_note-auto1-3)
The school has fielded a team since 1936, playing 925 total games (726 wins, 182 losses, 17 ties), producing an all-time winning percentage of 79% as of 2021.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_High_School#cite_note-4)

### State championships
*   Fort Hill has won 11 state football championships since the inception of the Maryland Public Secondary Schools Athletic Association state playoffs in 1974. By decade:   
    *   1975 (3A)  
    *   1997 (2A)  
    *   2013 (1A), 2014 (1A), 2015 (1A), 2016 (1A), 2018 (1A)  
    *   2021 (1A), 2022 (1A), 2023 (1A), 2024 (1A).[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_High_School#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_High_School#cite_note-6)

*   Fort Hill has a Maryland state record of most undefeated regular seasons at 21:   
    *   **40s-60s:** 1948, 1950, 1957, 1958, 1963,  
    *   **70s-90s:** 1973, 1975, 1977, 1990, 1994, 1995, 1997  
    *   **2000-2020:** 2000, 2009, 2011, 2013, 2014, 2016, 2018  
    *   **Since 2021:** 2021, 2023.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_High_School#cite_note-7)

### State championships
*   Fort Hill has a Maryland state record of most undefeated seasons overall at 14:   
    *   **40s-60s:** 1948, 1950, 1957, 1958, 1963  
    *   **70s-90s:** 1973, 1975, 1997  
    *   **2000s:** 2013, 2014, 2016, 2018, 2021, 2023.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_High_School#cite_note-8)
The school gymnasium is used for league basketball.
Greenway Avenue Stadium, located at the school, was constructed in the 1930s by the Public Works Administration as part of President Roosevelt's New Deal and was built for the high school as _Fort Hill Stadium_. The stadium, since renamed as Greenway Avenue stadium and shared with Allegany High School, is considered to be an historic landmark. A $7 million renovation project to update and expand the 70-year-old facility has been completed.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_High_School#cite_note-9)

Title: Fort Hill-Dunbar, through the years
Chunks: 0,1,2,3
Sep. 11—Rivalries come in all shapes and sizes.
Some are marked by their frequency and tradition — think Fort Hill-Allegany or Allegany-Keyser, both spanning more than 100 games. Others, like the Steelers-Raiders in the '70s and Patriots-Colts during the 2000s, blossomed due to recurrent high-stakes matchups.
Advertisement
Fort Hill and Dunbar fit into that second group. All six of their meetings have come with championships on the line: five in state title games and once in a semifinal.
That will change at Morgan State on Friday. For the first time in history, Fort Hill and Dunbar, holders of a combined 23 championships between them, link up in the regular season.
Due to reclassification, the teams won't play for a title any time soon.
Since the state moved to a six class system in 2021, Dunbar and Fort Hill have won all three state titles in Class 2A/1A and 1A, respectively.
That doesn't mean Friday's contest is without stakes. The winner will hold the longest win streak in the state of Maryland.
Advertisement
Dunbar already does, boasting 38 wins in a row, while Fort Hill is second with 22 consecutive triumphs.
The Poets also have their sights on the all-time Maryland record for consecutive victories of 53, set by Damascus from 2015-18, which they could achieve next season.
Furthermore, there is intrigue surrounding the timing of the matchup, as both are in position to tie a state record with a fourth consecutive state championship this year.
Fort Hill shares the current high mark with Urbana (1998-01), winning four in a row under Hall of Fame coach Todd Appel from 2013-16.
Before getting into the Dunbar-Fort Hill series, in which the Poets hold a 5-1 edge, it's worth highlighting the last time a Cumberland school played, and beat, the Baltimore City power.
Advertisement
In Week 1 of 2017, Allegany welcomed Dunbar to Greenway Avenue Stadium and the two produced an all-time offensive classic that featured a combined 91 points, 43 first downs and 906 yards of offense.

Elisha Llewellyn and Karson Robinette accounted for nearly 500 yards between them, and Allegany sent the Poets back East packing with a 49-42 defeat.
The loss lit a fire in Dunbar, whose season ended with hardware earned from toppling the Campers' crosstown rival, but more on that later.
We'll begin our journey with Fort Hill's lone victory in the series and then travel back in time chronologically.
Advertisement
1997
Fort Hill 22, Dunbar 6
Led by the rushing of hard-nosed fullback Josh Page, Fort Hill avenged its loss to the Poets three years prior to end a 22-year championship drought in College Park.
The 6-foot-3, 220-pound back pounded Dunbar to the tune of 125 yards and two touchdowns on 33 carries. He finished his career with then-state records in 71 touchdowns and 438 points and an area record 4,987 rushing yards.
Fort Hill finished with a 13-0 record punctuated by the Class 2A title.
The result is the most lopsided in series history. Dunbar has won by 15 twice, and the last three meetings have been decided by six points or less.
Advertisement
It was the lone championship for Hall of Fame coach Mike Calhoun, who guided Fort Hill to five title games and four in his final five years. He finished with a 122-31 record.
2017
Dunbar 30, Fort Hill 26
With Fort Hill aiming for a record fifth consecutive state championship, Dunbar scored the second-half's lone touchdown, an 87-yard passing score in the third quarter, to deny the Sentinels in Annapolis.
Fort Hill (12-2) led 26-22 at halftime, but Dunbar adjusted to load the box and deny Troy Banks, who finished with 153 yards on 35 carries.
Dunbar (12-1) won the second half 8-0 and the game on Jared Lewis' short pass to Ryan Wood that resulted in an 87-yard house call.
Advertisement

The clash of styles was evident by the teams' scoring drives. Dunbar scored six points on a 68-yard run and passes for 60, 63 and 87 yards. Fort Hill on sustained 69-, 77- and 88-yard series.
Luke Hamilton, Carter Swan, Wyatt Brehm, Kaleb Harden and Braeden Smith led the Fort Hill defense.
The championship game appearance was the fifth of six in a row for Fort Hill under Hall of Fame coach Todd Appel, a state record. Appel finished with a 142-16 record and won five Class 1A state titles.
Appel is now the defensive coordinator at Stephen Decatur in Berlin, which he helped to a Class 2A state championship last year. It was the school's first.
Advertisement
2010
Dunbar 20, Fort Hill 14
In the lone matchup that wasn't for a state championship, little 5-foot-6, 140-pound Dunbar quarterback Kevin Estep snuck over the line with three seconds left at Baltimore Poly's Lumsden Scott Stadium to advance to the title game.
The touchdown came on fourth-and-goal and broke a 14-all tie. Fort Hill drew even on a 30-yard pop pass from Dylan Clay to Justin Dawson with 5:20 left in the third quarter. Joe Howser found Dawson on the two-point conversion.
Garrett Clay finished with 118 yards on 16 carries to top Fort Hill (9-4).
"They pushed us around," Dunbar coach Lawrence Smith recalled at the time. "They pushed us down the field. Our defense was sucking wind."
Advertisement
Fort Hill gave a miraculous defensive effort to hold down a Dunbar (12-1) team led by workhorse back Epenetus Henriques, who had 33 carries for 224 yards.
Dunbar went on to score 22 unanswered points in the championship game to defeat Havre de Grace, 22-12, and lift the Class 1A title.
2008
Dunbar 20, Fort Hill 19
Dunbar's Tavon Austin went down as one of, if not the greatest scholastic football player in state history, and Fort Hill was one stop short of doing the impossible.

The Poets (13-1) drove 91 yards in the final two minutes, and Austin went around the left side of his line for the winning two-point conversion. Jonathan Perry connected with Sean Farr for the touchdown at Baltimore's M&T Bank Stadium.
Advertisement
Austin still holds career state records for total offense (9,258), rushing yards (7,962), points (790) and touchdowns (123). He rushed for 2,660 yards and 34 touchdowns on just 218 carries as a senior.
Against Fort Hill (11-2), he finished with 191 yards on 28 carries and scored a pair of touchdowns to clinch a three-peat against Cumberland city schools. Dunbar beat Fort Hill in the '06 title game and Allegany in '07.
Austin would go on to an All-American career at West Virginia and was selected eighth overall by the Rams. He played nine NFL seasons, officially retiring this August.
It was a heartbreaker for Fort Hill, which missed a 37-yard field goal with two minutes to go that would have iced the game.
Advertisement
The closeness of the game shocked coach Smith, whose Poets got all they could handle from the Sentinels in Appel's first season.
Marcus Lashley scored two touchdowns for Fort Hill, and Eric Howser accounted for the other.
2006
Dunbar 38, Fort Hill 23
Dunbar racked up 549 yards of offense led by Austin and Marice Portee to turn back Barry Lattimer's Fort Hill at Ravens Stadium.
The duo accounted for a combined 453 yards of offense. Fort Hill held Austin to just eight rushing yards on four carries in the first half, but Marice Portee exploded for 195 yards to keep the Poets afloat until Austin found his rhythm.
Advertisement
Austin rushed for 113 yards and three scores in the second half, and Portee led the way with 237 yards for the game.
Fort Hill (12-2) turned the ball over three times, and Dunbar (11-3) turned two of those into touchdowns.
Drew Yurko paced Fort Hill with 109 yards and a touchdown on 17 carries. Scott Rice added two scores.

Rise and Reclaim is alive and well in Cumberland, Maryland, as the Fort Hillfootballteam continued its redemption tour with a heart-stopping 43-42 victory over Bridgeport (W.Va.) on Friday.

## **Four Touchdowns in Less Than 8 Minutes**
The game featured four touchdowns in the final 7:36, a successful two-point conversion in the closing minute, and a missed field goal on the final play in one of the most dramatic finishes this season.
The victory marked the second straight week Fort Hill avenged a 2025 loss as it continues its quest to reclaim its position as the state’s top 1A program. Fort Hill won four straight state championships before falling in last year’s state final, prompting the “Rise and Reclaim” motto for 2026. Fort Hill took a big step in that direction last week with a 35-21 victory over Hollidaysburg (Pa.). But Bridgeport was a different kind of monster.
Last year, Bridgeport handed Fort Hill a 49-14 thrashing in West Virginia, Fort Hill’s most lopsided regular-season loss since 2012. Friday’s rematch at Greenway Avenue Stadium carried historical significance, marking Bridgeport’s first game outside West Virginia after 1,098 consecutive in-state contests dating to 1921. The Sentinels again found themselves in trouble Friday, falling behind 21-7 before Bridgeport scored on a 70-yard play in the closing seconds of the second quarter to take a 28-14 halftime lead.
Fort Hill rallied to tie the game at 28 in the third quarter, setting up a wild finish.
Bridgeport took a 35-28 lead with 7:36 remaining, but Brady O’Neal answered 62 seconds later with a 78-yard touchdown pass to Carson Bender. Bridgeport again surged ahead, 42-35, before a three-minute Fort Hill drive was capped by Neek Taylor’s 7-yard scoring run, making it 42-41. There was no hesitation about going for two.
“When we started the next drive [down 42-35], everyone knew we’d be going for two,” Fort Hill coach Zach Alkire said.
After Bridgeport burned a timeout, Fort Hill called a quick pitch to the left. The wing got just enough of a block to give Taylor the room he needed to barely cross the goal line, putting Fort Hill ahead 43-42 with 51 seconds remaining.

## **Four Touchdowns in Less Than 8 Minutes**
Bridgeport quickly moved into field-goal range, aided by a defensive pass-interference penalty. An encroachment penalty moved the final attempt from 44 to 39 yards, but the kick had the distance and sailed just wide right, sending Fort Hill to 5-0.
“The sideline went nuts,” Alkire said. “Kids running off the field, hugging. There was a lot of excitement, and we needed that.”

## **100 Wins, 46 Years in the Making**
Washington defeated Nandua (Va.), 20-10, in a contest that could easily be overlooked among the more than 100 games played by Maryland high schools this past weekend.
For Washington, however, it was anything but ordinary. The victory marked the program’s 100th varsity win — a milestone 46 years in the making.
Washington launched its first varsity football team in 1980 and lost its debut 42-0 to James M. Bennett. That proved to be a sign of things to come.
Except for the COVID-19 pandemic season in 2020, Washington has put a varsity team on the field every year since 1980. During that time, Washington has had only two winning seasons: 7-4 in 1989 and 8-5 in 2003. Yet the program has persevered despite finishing at or near the bottom of the Bayside standings for much of its history.
Perhaps the times are changing for this tiny school, which has about 600 students in grades 8-12.
Alec Meintzer inherited the program in 2023 while it was mired in an 18-game losing streak. That streak eventually reached 38 games before Washington broke through with a 16-6 victory over North East-Cecil last season. The win sparked something bigger: Washington finished 5-5, its first non-losing season since 2003.
Meintzer stepped down after the season, and Tremont White has taken over. This year’s team is officially 2-2, as the MPSSAA ruled that a scheduled season opener at Northampton (Va.) was a no-contest since the game was not played.
Now Washington has a chance to reach 3-2 for the first time since 1998 when it faces Arcadia (Va.) on Friday. The Jaguars defeated Arcadia, 36-16, last season.

## **Forfeits, No-Contests Becoming an Unwanted Trend**
The Maryland high school football season has reached the halfway point, and an unusual number of games have disappeared from the schedule because of forfeits, no-contests, or teams dropping games altogether.
The latest came this past weekend in Prince George’s County. According to one of the head coaches, an altercation in the handshake line after the Oxon Hill-Potomac game in Week 4 resulted in both teams forfeiting their Week 5 contests. The two teams will also play their remaining games this season on Saturdays.
According to one of the head coaches, an altercation in the handshake line following the Oxon Hill-Potomac game in Week 4 resulted in both teams forfeiting their Week 5 contests.
It is the latest in a growing list of unusual circumstances that have taken games off the schedule this season.
North Point and Westlake forfeited their season openers in Charles County because of what was termed out-of-season contact violations. Maryland School for the Deaf received a forfeit victory when its scheduled opponent disbanded the week of the game. Annapolis Area Christian has forfeited two games because of a lack of healthy players.
Weather has also played a role. Northampton (Va.) canceled its scheduled game at Washington because of what was described as “extreme heat,” while weather-related no-contests cost Flowers and Wise games from their schedules.
The situation has been particularly interesting at Edmondson-Westside. Through five weeks, the team has played only two games. One scheduled game was a forfeit, and two others were never played after Hancock and Benjamin Franklin dropped their football programs before the season.
This past weekend, Sidwell Friends, which rejoined the Mid-Atlantic Conference this season, forfeited its league opener at St. James on Saturday, citing not enough healthy players.
Meanwhile, Central Maryland Christian, down to 18 players, has reduced its regular-season schedule to four games.
While the reasons are varied, the result is the same: fewer opportunities for players to compete and an increasingly unpredictable high school football schedule.

## **Crofton Remains Unbeaten**
Crofton was featured early this season after what was then considered an upset victory over Old Mill.
Now, the Wildcats have established themselves as the team to beat in Anne Arundel County. Crofton is the county’s lone 5-0 team and one of just 21 undefeated teams remaining in the MPSSAA.
Dominic Jackson delivered the latest heroics, scoring on a 3-yard run to lift Crofton to a 20-17 overtime victory over Chesapeake-AA.
The teams tied at 14 after regulation. Gary Windsor gave Chesapeake-AA a 17-14 lead in the first overtime with a 27-yard field goal, but Crofton answered with a touchdown to complete the comeback and remain unbeaten.

## **Got Your Number**
Northwestern-PG edged Bladensburg, 22-20, over the weekend, marking the third consecutive year the Wildcats have beaten the Mustangs.
While the streak is notable, it is even more remarkable that Bladensburg is the only team Northwestern-PG has beaten since 2019.
Since midseason 2019, Northwestern-PG is 4-2 against Bladensburg but 0-53 against all other opponents. The Wildcats’ last victory over anyone other than Bladensburg came on Oct. 12, 2019, when Northwestern-PG thrashed DuVal, 47-6.

texts.0: Rise and Reclaim is alive and well in Cumberland, Maryland, as the Fort Hillfootballteam continued its redemption tour with a heart-stopping 43-42 victory over Bridgeport (W.Va.) on Friday.
texts.1:
## **Four Touchdowns in Less Than 8 Minutes**
The game featured four touchdowns in the final 7:36, a successful two-point conversion in the closing minute, and a missed field goal on the final play in one of the most dramatic finishes this season.
The victory marked the second straight week Fort Hill avenged a 2025 loss as it continues its quest to reclaim its position as the state’s top 1A program. Fort Hill won four straight state championships before falling in last year’s state final, prompting the “Rise and Reclaim” motto for 2026. Fort Hill took a big step in that direction last week with a 35-21 victory over Hollidaysburg (Pa.). But Bridgeport was a different kind of monster.
Last year, Bridgeport handed Fort Hill a 49-14 thrashing in West Virginia, Fort Hill’s most lopsided regular-season loss since 2012. Friday’s rematch at Greenway Avenue Stadium carried historical significance, marking Bridgeport’s first game outside West Virginia after 1,098 consecutive in-state contests dating to 1921. The Sentinels again found themselves in trouble Friday, falling behind 21-7 before Bridgeport scored on a 70-yard play in the closing seconds of the second quarter to take a 28-14 halftime lead.
Fort Hill rallied to tie the game at 28 in the third quarter, setting up a wild finish.
Bridgeport took a 35-28 lead with 7:36 remaining, but Brady O’Neal answered 62 seconds later with a 78-yard touchdown pass to Carson Bender. Bridgeport again surged ahead, 42-35, before a three-minute Fort Hill drive was capped by Neek Taylor’s 7-yard scoring run, making it 42-41. There was no hesitation about going for two.
“When we started the next drive [down 42-35], everyone knew we’d be going for two,” Fort Hill coach Zach Alkire said.
After Bridgeport burned a timeout, Fort Hill called a quick pitch to the left. The wing got just enough of a block to give Taylor the room he needed to barely cross the goal line, putting Fort Hill ahead 43-42 with 51 seconds remaining.

**Fort Hill High School** is a four-year public high school in Cumberland, Maryland, United States, serving 780 students in grades 9 through 12. Fort Hill is part of Allegany County Public Schools**.**
Fort Hill High School was one of three local New Deal projects. Fort Hill High school was a Public Works Administration project. Nearby Constitution Park and Greeway Avenue Stadium were Works Progress Administration projects
New Deal funding relating to Fort Hill was initiated in November 1934 and September 1935, when the PWA committed federal funds not to exceed $230,000. The project was labeled PWA Docket #7323.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_High_School#cite_note-2)

Sep. 11—Rivalries come in all shapes and sizes.
Some are marked by their frequency and tradition — think Fort Hill-Allegany or Allegany-Keyser, both spanning more than 100 games. Others, like the Steelers-Raiders in the '70s and Patriots-Colts during the 2000s, blossomed due to recurrent high-stakes matchups.
Advertisement
Fort Hill and Dunbar fit into that second group. All six of their meetings have come with championships on the line: five in state title games and once in a semifinal.
That will change at Morgan State on Friday. For the first time in history, Fort Hill and Dunbar, holders of a combined 23 championships between them, link up in the regular season.
Due to reclassification, the teams won't play for a title any time soon.
Since the state moved to a six class system in 2021, Dunbar and Fort Hill have won all three state titles in Class 2A/1A and 1A, respectively.
That doesn't mean Friday's contest is without stakes. The winner will hold the longest win streak in the state of Maryland.
Advertisement
Dunbar already does, boasting 38 wins in a row, while Fort Hill is second with 22 consecutive triumphs.
The Poets also have their sights on the all-time Maryland record for consecutive victories of 53, set by Damascus from 2015-18, which they could achieve next season.
Furthermore, there is intrigue surrounding the timing of the matchup, as both are in position to tie a state record with a fourth consecutive state championship this year.
Fort Hill shares the current high mark with Urbana (1998-01), winning four in a row under Hall of Fame coach Todd Appel from 2013-16.
Before getting into the Dunbar-Fort Hill series, in which the Poets hold a 5-1 edge, it's worth highlighting the last time a Cumberland school played, and beat, the Baltimore City power.
Advertisement
In Week 1 of 2017, Allegany welcomed Dunbar to Greenway Avenue Stadium and the two produced an all-time offensive classic that featured a combined 91 points, 43 first downs and 906 yards of offense.
texts.1:
Elisha Llewellyn and Karson Robinette accounted for nearly 500 yards between them, and Allegany sent the Poets back East packing with a 49-42 defeat.
The loss lit a fire in Dunbar, whose season ended with hardware earned from toppling the Campers' crosstown rival, but more on that later.
We'll begin our journey with Fort Hill's lone victory in the series and then travel back in time chronologically.
Advertisement
1997
Fort Hill 22, Dunbar 6
Led by the rushing of hard-nosed fullback Josh Page, Fort Hill avenged its loss to the Poets three years prior to end a 22-year championship drought in College Park.
The 6-foot-3, 220-pound back pounded Dunbar to the tune of 125 yards and two touchdowns on 33 carries. He finished his career with then-state records in 71 touchdowns and 438 points and an area record 4,987 rushing yards.
Fort Hill finished with a 13-0 record punctuated by the Class 2A title.
The result is the most lopsided in series history. Dunbar has won by 15 twice, and the last three meetings have been decided by six points or less.
Advertisement
It was the lone championship for Hall of Fame coach Mike Calhoun, who guided Fort Hill to five title games and four in his final five years. He finished with a 122-31 record.
2017
Dunbar 30, Fort Hill 26
With Fort Hill aiming for a record fifth consecutive state championship, Dunbar scored the second-half's lone touchdown, an 87-yard passing score in the third quarter, to deny the Sentinels in Annapolis.
Fort Hill (12-2) led 26-22 at halftime, but Dunbar adjusted to load the box and deny Troy Banks, who finished with 153 yards on 35 carries.
Dunbar (12-1) won the second half 8-0 and the game on Jared Lewis' short pass to Ryan Wood that resulted in an 87-yard house call.
Advertisement
texts.2:
The clash of styles was evident by the teams' scoring drives. Dunbar scored six points on a 68-yard run and passes for 60, 63 and 87 yards. Fort Hill on sustained 69-, 77- and 88-yard series.
Luke Hamilton, Carter Swan, Wyatt Brehm, Kaleb Harden and Braeden Smith led the Fort Hill defense.
The championship game appearance was the fifth of six in a row for Fort Hill under Hall of Fame coach Todd Appel, a state record. Appel finished with a 142-16 record and won five Class 1A state titles.
Appel is now the defensive coordinator at Stephen Decatur in Berlin, which he helped to a Class 2A state championship last year. It was the school's first.
Advertisement
2010
Dunbar 20, Fort Hill 14
In the lone matchup that wasn't for a state championship, little 5-foot-6, 140-pound Dunbar quarterback Kevin Estep snuck over the line with three seconds left at Baltimore Poly's Lumsden Scott Stadium to advance to the title game.
The touchdown came on fourth-and-goal and broke a 14-all tie. Fort Hill drew even on a 30-yard pop pass from Dylan Clay to Justin Dawson with 5:20 left in the third quarter. Joe Howser found Dawson on the two-point conversion.
Garrett Clay finished with 118 yards on 16 carries to top Fort Hill (9-4).
"They pushed us around," Dunbar coach Lawrence Smith recalled at the time. "They pushed us down the field. Our defense was sucking wind."
Advertisement
Fort Hill gave a miraculous defensive effort to hold down a Dunbar (12-1) team led by workhorse back Epenetus Henriques, who had 33 carries for 224 yards.
Dunbar went on to score 22 unanswered points in the championship game to defeat Havre de Grace, 22-12, and lift the Class 1A title.
2008
Dunbar 20, Fort Hill 19
Dunbar's Tavon Austin went down as one of, if not the greatest scholastic football player in state history, and Fort Hill was one stop short of doing the impossible.
texts.3:
The Poets (13-1) drove 91 yards in the final two minutes, and Austin went around the left side of his line for the winning two-point conversion. Jonathan Perry connected with Sean Farr for the touchdown at Baltimore's M&T Bank Stadium.

Rise and Reclaim is alive and well in Cumberland, Maryland, as the Fort Hillfootballteam continued its redemption tour with a heart-stopping 43-42 victory over Bridgeport (W.Va.) on Friday.

## **Four Touchdowns in Less Than 8 Minutes**
The game featured four touchdowns in the final 7:36, a successful two-point conversion in the closing minute, and a missed field goal on the final play in one of the most dramatic finishes this season.
The victory marked the second straight week Fort Hill avenged a 2025 loss as it continues its quest to reclaim its position as the state’s top 1A program. Fort Hill won four straight state championships before falling in last year’s state final, prompting the “Rise and Reclaim” motto for 2026. Fort Hill took a big step in that direction last week with a 35-21 victory over Hollidaysburg (Pa.). But Bridgeport was a different kind of monster.
Last year, Bridgeport handed Fort Hill a 49-14 thrashing in West Virginia, Fort Hill’s most lopsided regular-season loss since 2012. Friday’s rematch at Greenway Avenue Stadium carried historical significance, marking Bridgeport’s first game outside West Virginia after 1,098 consecutive in-state contests dating to 1921. The Sentinels again found themselves in trouble Friday, falling behind 21-7 before Bridgeport scored on a 70-yard play in the closing seconds of the second quarter to take a 28-14 halftime lead.
Fort Hill rallied to tie the game at 28 in the third quarter, setting up a wild finish.
Bridgeport took a 35-28 lead with 7:36 remaining, but Brady O’Neal answered 62 seconds later with a 78-yard touchdown pass to Carson Bender. Bridgeport again surged ahead, 42-35, before a three-minute Fort Hill drive was capped by Neek Taylor’s 7-yard scoring run, making it 42-41. There was no hesitation about going for two.
“When we started the next drive [down 42-35], everyone knew we’d be going for two,” Fort Hill coach Zach Alkire said.
After Bridgeport burned a timeout, Fort Hill called a quick pitch to the left. The wing got just enough of a block to give Taylor the room he needed to barely cross the goal line, putting Fort Hill ahead 43-42 with 51 seconds remaining.

## **Four Touchdowns in Less Than 8 Minutes**
Bridgeport quickly moved into field-goal range, aided by a defensive pass-interference penalty. An encroachment penalty moved the final attempt from 44 to 39 yards, but the kick had the distance and sailed just wide right, sending Fort Hill to 5-0.
“The sideline went nuts,” Alkire said. “Kids running off the field, hugging. There was a lot of excitement, and we needed that.”

## **100 Wins, 46 Years in the Making**
Washington defeated Nandua (Va.), 20-10, in a contest that could easily be overlooked among the more than 100 games played by Maryland high schools this past weekend.
For Washington, however, it was anything but ordinary. The victory marked the program’s 100th varsity win — a milestone 46 years in the making.
Washington launched its first varsity football team in 1980 and lost its debut 42-0 to James M. Bennett. That proved to be a sign of things to come.
Except for the COVID-19 pandemic season in 2020, Washington has put a varsity team on the field every year since 1980. During that time, Washington has had only two winning seasons: 7-4 in 1989 and 8-5 in 2003. Yet the program has persevered despite finishing at or near the bottom of the Bayside standings for much of its history.
Perhaps the times are changing for this tiny school, which has about 600 students in grades 8-12.
Alec Meintzer inherited the program in 2023 while it was mired in an 18-game losing streak. That streak eventually reached 38 games before Washington broke through with a 16-6 victory over North East-Cecil last season. The win sparked something bigger: Washington finished 5-5, its first non-losing season since 2003.
Meintzer stepped down after the season, and Tremont White has taken over. This year’s team is officially 2-2, as the MPSSAA ruled that a scheduled season opener at Northampton (Va.) was a no-contest since the game was not played.
Now Washington has a chance to reach 3-2 for the first time since 1998 when it faces Arcadia (Va.) on Friday. The Jaguars defeated Arcadia, 36-16, last season.

## **Forfeits, No-Contests Becoming an Unwanted Trend**
The Maryland high school football season has reached the halfway point, and an unusual number of games have disappeared from the schedule because of forfeits, no-contests, or teams dropping games altogether.
The latest came this past weekend in Prince George’s County. According to one of the head coaches, an altercation in the handshake line after the Oxon Hill-Potomac game in Week 4 resulted in both teams forfeiting their Week 5 contests. The two teams will also play their remaining games this season on Saturdays.

This past weekend, Sidwell Friends, which rejoined the Mid-Atlantic Conference this season, forfeited its league opener at St. James on Saturday, citing not enough healthy players.

While the reasons are varied, the result is the same: fewer opportunities for players to compete and an increasingly unpredictable high school football schedule.

The teams tied at 14 after regulation. Gary Windsor gave Chesapeake-AA a 17-14 lead in the first overtime with a 27-yard field goal, but Crofton answered with a touchdown to complete the comeback and remain unbeaten.

While the streak is notable, it is even more remarkable that Bladensburg is the only team Northwestern-PG has beaten since 2019.

Sep. 11—Rivalries come in all shapes and sizes.
Some are marked by their frequency and tradition — think Fort Hill-Allegany or Allegany-Keyser, both spanning more than 100 games. Others, like the Steelers-Raiders in the '70s and Patriots-Colts during the 2000s, blossomed due to recurrent high-stakes matchups.
Advertisement
Fort Hill and Dunbar fit into that second group. All six of their meetings have come with championships on the line: five in state title games and once in a semifinal.
That will change at Morgan State on Friday. For the first time in history, Fort Hill and Dunbar, holders of a combined 23 championships between them, link up in the regular season.
Due to reclassification, the teams won't play for a title any time soon.
Since the state moved to a six class system in 2021, Dunbar and Fort Hill have won all three state titles in Class 2A/1A and 1A, respectively.
That doesn't mean Friday's contest is without stakes. The winner will hold the longest win streak in the state of Maryland.
Advertisement
Dunbar already does, boasting 38 wins in a row, while Fort Hill is second with 22 consecutive triumphs.
The Poets also have their sights on the all-time Maryland record for consecutive victories of 53, set by Damascus from 2015-18, which they could achieve next season.
Furthermore, there is intrigue surrounding the timing of the matchup, as both are in position to tie a state record with a fourth consecutive state championship this year.
Fort Hill shares the current high mark with Urbana (1998-01), winning four in a row under Hall of Fame coach Todd Appel from 2013-16.
Before getting into the Dunbar-Fort Hill series, in which the Poets hold a 5-1 edge, it's worth highlighting the last time a Cumberland school played, and beat, the Baltimore City power.
Advertisement
In Week 1 of 2017, Allegany welcomed Dunbar to Greenway Avenue Stadium and the two produced an all-time offensive classic that featured a combined 91 points, 43 first downs and 906 yards of offense.

Elisha Llewellyn and Karson Robinette accounted for nearly 500 yards between them, and Allegany sent the Poets back East packing with a 49-42 defeat.
The loss lit a fire in Dunbar, whose season ended with hardware earned from toppling the Campers' crosstown rival, but more on that later.
We'll begin our journey with Fort Hill's lone victory in the series and then travel back in time chronologically.
Advertisement
1997
Fort Hill 22, Dunbar 6
Led by the rushing of hard-nosed fullback Josh Page, Fort Hill avenged its loss to the Poets three years prior to end a 22-year championship drought in College Park.
The 6-foot-3, 220-pound back pounded Dunbar to the tune of 125 yards and two touchdowns on 33 carries. He finished his career with then-state records in 71 touchdowns and 438 points and an area record 4,987 rushing yards.
Fort Hill finished with a 13-0 record punctuated by the Class 2A title.
The result is the most lopsided in series history. Dunbar has won by 15 twice, and the last three meetings have been decided by six points or less.
Advertisement
It was the lone championship for Hall of Fame coach Mike Calhoun, who guided Fort Hill to five title games and four in his final five years. He finished with a 122-31 record.
2017
Dunbar 30, Fort Hill 26
With Fort Hill aiming for a record fifth consecutive state championship, Dunbar scored the second-half's lone touchdown, an 87-yard passing score in the third quarter, to deny the Sentinels in Annapolis.
Fort Hill (12-2) led 26-22 at halftime, but Dunbar adjusted to load the box and deny Troy Banks, who finished with 153 yards on 35 carries.
Dunbar (12-1) won the second half 8-0 and the game on Jared Lewis' short pass to Ryan Wood that resulted in an 87-yard house call.
Advertisement

The clash of styles was evident by the teams' scoring drives. Dunbar scored six points on a 68-yard run and passes for 60, 63 and 87 yards. Fort Hill on sustained 69-, 77- and 88-yard series.
Luke Hamilton, Carter Swan, Wyatt Brehm, Kaleb Harden and Braeden Smith led the Fort Hill defense.
The championship game appearance was the fifth of six in a row for Fort Hill under Hall of Fame coach Todd Appel, a state record. Appel finished with a 142-16 record and won five Class 1A state titles.
Appel is now the defensive coordinator at Stephen Decatur in Berlin, which he helped to a Class 2A state championship last year. It was the school's first.
Advertisement
2010
Dunbar 20, Fort Hill 14
In the lone matchup that wasn't for a state championship, little 5-foot-6, 140-pound Dunbar quarterback Kevin Estep snuck over the line with three seconds left at Baltimore Poly's Lumsden Scott Stadium to advance to the title game.

### Men's Cross Country
[edit]
UC Davis captured its first Big West Championship in 2010 when individual conference champion Jonathan Peterson led the Aggies to their historic victory.
Records_[dead link_]
UC Davis added beach volleyball ahead of the 2019 season, joining Equestrian as the department's newest sports. The Aggies opened their historic first season with a 2–0 record and enjoyed success in their most recent campaign, posting their best start to a season (9–0) in program history.
UC Davis added field hockey ahead of the 2009 season, competing in the NorPac conference. The Aggies joined the American East in 2015 and remain in the conference heading into 2023. UC Davis has not posted a winning season since the program's inception, but finished just one game below .500 (8–9) in 2019.

### Women's Track and Field
[edit]
In less than half a decade, UC Davis women's track & field boasted three finalists – including two winners – for the NCAA Woman of the Year Award, which honors excellence and leadership in athletics, academics and in the community. Founded in 1991, the award stands as one of the highest honors that national governing body bestows upon an individual. Since then, UC Davis is the only Division II institution to have won the award and is one of just two schools to have three winners (Aggie lacrosse player Kelly Albin captured the honor in 2004). Hundreds of student-athletes are nominated annually, from which one winner is chosen for each state plus the District of Columbia and Puerto Rico. From those 52 state-level honorees, the NCAA selects 10 finalists. The winner is then chosen at an annual televised banquet. Remarkably, the Aggies’ All-American 4x400 relay team at the 1999 NCAA Outdoor Championships featured three finalists: 2001 finalist Kameelah Elarms was the leadoff runner, 2002 winner Tanisha Silas ran the third leg and 1999 winner Jamila Demby served as the anchor.
Records_[dead link_]
UC Davis added Equestrian ahead of the 2019 season and the program instantly enjoyed success, earning their first ECAC Championship in 2023. The young team repeated their conference championship in 2024, and qualified for Nationals for the first time in program history as the #8 ranked team in the nation. It was announced on January 9, 2026, that following the 2026 season, Equestrian would be downgraded to club status, and STUNT would be elevated to varsity status in its place.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UC_Davis_Aggies#cite_note-19)

### Women's Track and Field
UC Davis women's golf is led by the three-time Big West Golfer of the Year and former LPGA Tour professional Demi Runas. Runas was the first Aggie to earn her LPGA Tour card. The Aggies have posted 23 team wins as well as 22 individual victories since the program started in 2005, also making four NCAA Tournament appearances (2008, 2011, 2013, 2015) over that time.
Led by Cal Aggie Athletics Hall of Fame student-athlete Tanya Ho, UC Davis gymnastics earned their first conference title since 2015 after a brilliant 2023 campaign. Ho guided the Aggies to the MPSF title as the No. 2 championship seed with a team national qualifying score of 195.965. UC Davis broke 196 in five meets, including the 196.200 en route to the team title. The Aggies totaled three of the MPSF's top-nine all-time scores in the final month of the regular season, including the No. 2 all-time ranking of 196.750. The last eight meets of the season all went for at least 195.250.
Records_[dead link_]
UC Davis' six conference wins in 2022 were the most by any UCD team since joining the Big West. UC Davis women's soccer is yet to win a conference title at the Division I level.

### Women's Cross Country
[edit]
UC Davis has won three Big West Conference titles (2011, 2014, 2021) since it ascended to the Division I level in 2007.
Records_[dead link_]
In March, 2020, UC Davis women's tennis also earned an NCAA Public Recognition Award for an outstanding Academic Progress Rate (APR) by posting its 12th perfect score in program history. This is the highest total of any men's or women's team sponsored by the Big West. As a Division II team, UC Davis captured the California Collegiate Athletic Association title three times in a row from 1999 to 2002.
UC Davis became a Big 12 affiliate member for that conference's first season of women's lacrosse in 2024–25, following the 2024 collapse of its former women's lacrosse home of the Pac-12 Conference. The Aggies had only joined Pac-12 women's lacrosse in 2023–24. Led by three-time Mountain Pacific Sports Federation (MPSF) Coach of the Year (2018, 2019, 2021), Suzanne Isidor captured her first conference title in 2021, leading the Aggies to a program-best 12–4 record.
UC Davis has effectively been a partner of fellow California school San Diego State, with both teams having been in MPSF women's lacrosse until that conference dropped women's lacrosse after the 2021 season. Both played as independents for two seasons until joining Pac-12 women's lacrosse for the 2024 season. The Aggies faced five Pac-12 opponents in 2022, posting wins over Cal and Oregon while also going 1–1 against San Diego State.
UC Davis women's volleyball ascended to the Division I level ahead of the 2004 season and have not won a conference title since the reclassification. Head Coach Dan Conners will enter his 10th season in 2023.
UC Davis Softball ascended to the Division I level in 2008 and claimed their first Big West Conference title in 2010 under Head Coach Karen Yoder.

### Women's Cross Country
UC Davis women's water polo earned a share of the Big West Conference title in 2009, their first championship in program history at the Division I level. In 2015, the Aggie made history by winning the Big West Conference Tournament to punch their ticket to the NCAA Tournament.

### Women's Swimming and Diving
[edit]
UC Davis swimming and diving has captured four MPSF titles (2011, 2013, 2014, 2016) since its ascension to the Division I level. In 2016, Hilvy Cheung raced in the NCAA prelim for the 200m butterfly, making the Aggies' first appearance on the national stage.
Records_[dead link_]
UC Davis has not won a national championship at the NCAA Division I level, but previously won eight national championships at the NCAA Division II level.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UC_Davis_Aggies#cite_note-champ-20)

### Women's Swimming and Diving
#### NCAA Division II National Championships
[edit]
Women's rowing team competing in 2017
*   Men's basketball: 1998  
*   Men's golf: 1979  
*   Women's rowing: 2002, 2003  
*   Softball: 2003  
*   Men's tennis: 1992  
*   Women's tennis: 1990, 1993

### Women's Swimming and Diving
#### Non-NCAA National Championships
[edit]
*   Women's gymnastics – Division III: 1981 (AIAW)  
*   Women's tennis – Division III: 1980, 1981 (AIAW)
